## Where a fit begins and ends {#sec-statmod-verdict}

Two questions bracket the fitting of @sec-statmod-inner and are not part of
it: where the iteration starts, and whether the point it stops at is the one
the model asks for.

### Where it begins {#sec-statmod-start}

The default is the maximum likelihood estimate of the model with every
covariate removed. The model with no covariates is the model with every slope
set to zero, so its estimate is exactly where the model with covariates
should begin, and it costs one small fit on an intercept-only design. Every
other coefficient starts at zero, which for a penalized block is where its
penalty is smallest.

Two adjustments make that usable where a naive intercept would not be, and
both were found by a fit that did not converge rather than by reasoning. An
offset is subtracted before the value is written, since without it a model
whose offset averages 6.74 begins at $e^{0.897 + 6.74} = 2080$ against a
sample mean of 2.45 — measured on a count model over person-years, 4.9
seconds and nine scoring iterations with the correction against more than
twenty-five minutes without. And the value is written to a **parametric**
intercept and to nothing else: a nonlinear term names the intercept of each
of its own parameters `(Intercept)` too, and those live on that parameter's
own chart rather than on the predictor's, so a predictor-scale value written
onto a parameter riding a log link became $e^{23.9} = 2.5 \times 10^{10}$.

A term with parameters of its own says where they start, since only the term
knows what zero means on its charts: a score-driven term's loadings begin at
a small positive value through their link rather than at zero, which for it
is the model without the term.

Where the likelihood is multimodal none of that is enough, and a global
search can be run once, before the fit. Three properties of it are worth
stating, because each is a decision rather than a detail. It runs **once**,
before the alternation between the coefficients and the hyperparameters
begins, and not inside the inner optimizer, where it would rerun at every
hyperparameter the outer search tries and return the same answer each time.
It runs on the **likelihood with the penalties off**, because what a starting
value has to get right is the basin, and at a probe value representing
nobody's choice a penalty would explore a different model. And it searches
only the **non-convex** coordinates, which the toolkit can name: a structural
term's parameters, the coefficients of a term that recomputes its own block,
and each equation's intercept. A smooth or a random effect is convex and the
scoring step reaches its optimum from anywhere; a penalized coordinate is
excluded wherever it sits, including inside a non-convex term, since on the
likelihood alone nothing identifies a deviation whose penalty is what
identifies it.

The hyperparameters cannot be searched from there at all. The objective is
the likelihood with the penalties off, in which a hyperparameter does not
appear, so no proposal could change one; a global search over them is a
search over the criterion of @sec-statmod-outer, where each proposal costs a
whole refit.

### Where it ends {#sec-statmod-certificate}

An optimizer's convergence flag says whether a search stopped on its own
rule, which is a statement about the search. What a reader wants is a
property of the point, and the two are not the same: measured on one model,
the default reported success at a criterion of $-1783.47$ while the same data
under a different optimizer reached $-1664.43$ and reported failure.

The certificate takes three readings at the reported point, independent of
the path taken to it: the outer criterion's gradient, how far the
coefficients sit above their own penalized mode, and which hyperparameters
have run to a boundary. It refits nothing.

The state comes from the gradient, and the mode error is reported beside it
rather than folded into it. That division is measured rather than chosen.
Across shapes the outer gradient separates by five orders of magnitude —
4.7e-07, 7.8e-07, 5.8e-05, 7.7e-05 and 3.0e-04 on fits that are right,
against 28.8 on one that is not — while the mode error does not: it reads
between 1.8e-16 and 6.1e-12 on four of them, 22.8 on the failing one, and
0.114 on a random-changepoint fit whose answer is right to a correlation of
0.9932. A number that does not separate cannot decide a state, and one that
says how far from the mode is worth more than a boolean hiding it.

```{r}
#| label: certificate
set.seed(24)
n_ce <- 400
d_ce <- data.frame(x = sort(runif(n_ce, -3, 3)),
                   g = factor(rep(1:20, length.out = n_ce)))
d_ce$y <- rnorm(n_ce, 1 + sin(1.2 * d_ce$x) + rnorm(20, sd = 0.5)[d_ce$g],
                exp(-0.7 + 0.25 * d_ce$x))

f_ce <- statmod(y ~ s(x, k = 8) + random(~ 1 | g) | sigma ~ s(x, k = 5),
                gaussian1_distrib(), d_ce)
ce <- statmod_certificate(f_ce)
c(state = ce$state, gradient = signif(ce$gradient, 3),
  mode_error = signif(ce$mode_error, 3), boundary = ce$boundary)
```

`boundary` is a certified state and not a complaint. A hyperparameter may run
to an edge and belong there, and here one has: the data were generated with
$\log\sigma$ linear in $x$, the scale's smooth is therefore being driven onto
its own null space, and its smoothing parameter reaches $3.2\times 10^{10}$.
The criterion is genuinely flat out there, so calling the fit unconverged
would be wrong.

A coordinate is reported as sitting at a boundary when its free value exceeds
a threshold **and** its own gradient component has already met the tolerance.
Because of that second condition the threshold cannot change the verdict: a
coordinate it moves out of the interior had already passed the test, so what
the threshold decides is how the point is described and never whether it is
certified. The default separates the measured cases with room on both sides,
coordinates that ran to an edge sitting at 9.3, 10.5 and 20.6 on the free
scale against 0.13, 0.30 and 2.01 for those that did not — and 24.2 for the
one above.

Two kinds of model have no outer gradient and are answered differently. One
with **no penalty** at all has no hyperparameter for a gradient to be about,
so the only question left is whether the inner fit reached its mode and the
mode error answers it. One whose only hyperparameters are **kinked** gets
neither reading and is reported as unknown: at a coefficient the penalty has
set to zero the score does not vanish but lies in the subdifferential, so the
mode error there is not a statement about being at a mode at all.
